steps.text: Rinse the kettle, then pour in 300 ml water (about one and a half glasses). Do not go above the max line.
Break the noodle cake into four pieces and drop them in with the onion and tomato.
Switch the kettle on. When it clicks off, leave the lid shut and let the noodles sit.
Open the lid, stir gently with a long spoon, and switch on again for one more boil.
Tip in the tastemaker sachet, stir until there are no lumps, and let it stand 1 minute.
Pour everything into your bowl and wash the kettle with hot water straight away while the starch is still soft.

tip.text: Watch the second boil. Starchy water foams up fast and can spill onto the base and trip your room's socket. Stand next to it and switch off the moment it rises.

steps.text: Place 2 eggs gently at the bottom of the kettle and add water until they are covered by about 2 cm.
Switch the kettle on and let it boil once.
Leave the lid closed after it clicks off. 10 minutes gives a firm yolk, 7 a jammy one.
While you wait, fill a mug or bowl with tap water to cool the eggs.
Lift the eggs out with a spoon into the cold water and leave them 2 minutes so the shell slips off.
Peel, halve lengthways, and sprinkle chaat masala, a pinch of salt and black pepper over the yolks.

tip.text: Eggs straight from a cold fridge can crack when the water heats. Leave them out for 10 minutes first, or lower them in once the water is warm.

title: Lemon Poha with Peanuts, No Stove

steps.text: Boil 300 ml water in the kettle.
Put 60 g thick poha in a sieve or steel tiffin, rinse once under the tap and drain it well.
Mix the turmeric, salt and sugar into 4 tablespoons of the hot water and sprinkle it over the poha. Toss and cover the tiffin.
Let the poha steam in its own heat until it turns soft.
Meanwhile chop the onion, green chilli and coriander as fine as you can.
Fluff the poha with a fork, fold in onion, chilli and peanuts, squeeze half a lemon over and top with sev and coriander.

tip.text: Do not soak poha in a bowl of water. It turns into paste in under a minute. A quick rinse plus a few spoons of hot water is all it needs.

steps.text: Put 50 g rolled oats (about half a cup) into a large mug or steel tumbler.
Add salt, chilli powder, turmeric and garam masala and stir them into the dry oats so the spice doesn't clump.
Boil 200 ml water in the kettle and pour it over the oats in one go.
Cover the mug with a saucer and leave it. The oats swell and thicken.
Stir in the chopped onion, tomato and coriander. Add a splash more hot water if it's too thick to stir.

tip.text: Use a big mug. Oats swell to almost double, and a full mug will overflow under the saucer and mess up your desk.

steps.text: Boil 500 ml water in the kettle and pour it over 50 g soya chunks in a bowl. Add a pinch of salt.
Cover and let the chunks soak until they are soft and doubled in size.
Drain, then rinse the chunks under cold tap water twice to wash out the beany smell.
Squeeze each handful hard between your palms until no more water drips out.
Tear the chunks in half and mix them with chopped onion, tomato and cucumber.
Add chaat masala, salt and the juice of half a lemon, toss, and finish with coriander.

tip.text: If you skip the squeezing, the chunks stay spongy and taste like cardboard soaked in water. Squeeze like you mean it.

steps.text: Put 60 g roasted vermicelli into a steel tiffin and break the long strands into finger-length pieces.
Add salt and turmeric and toss so every strand is coated.
Boil 250 ml water and pour just enough over the vermicelli to cover it.
Clamp the lid on and let it steam. It is done when a strand pinched between fingers has no white core.
Drain any water left at the bottom by tilting the tiffin against the lid.
Mix in the pickle oil and a little pickle for tadka flavour, then the peanuts, chopped chilli, torn curry leaves and lemon juice.

tip.text: Buy roasted vermicelli. Unroasted semiya turns gluey in hot water, and you can't roast it without a pan.

steps.text: Put 70 g couscous in a bowl with salt, chilli powder and the cumin seeds rubbed between your palms to crush them.
Pour in 100 ml boiling water from the kettle (just enough to cover by a few millimetres) and add the olive oil.
Cover with a plate and leave it alone.
Drain and rinse half a can of chickpeas (about 120 g) while the couscous steams.
Fluff the couscous with a fork, breaking every clump.
Fold in chickpeas, chopped onion and coriander, and squeeze over the lemon.

tip.text: Measure the water. Too much and couscous turns into porridge. The ratio is roughly 1 part couscous to 1.3 parts water by volume.

steps.text: Pour 70 ml boiling water over 50 g couscous with a pinch of salt and cover it.
Leave it to swell while you chop.
Dice the cucumber and tomato into small cubes the size of a chickpea.
Strip mint leaves from their stems and chop them with the coriander until very fine. You want almost a heap of green.
Fluff the couscous, let it cool for 2 minutes, then fold in the vegetables and herbs.
Dress with the juice of one whole lemon, olive oil, salt and pepper. It should taste sharp.

tip.text: Adding herbs to steaming-hot couscous wilts them black. Wait until you can touch the couscous comfortably.

steps.text: Put 75 g hakka noodles (half a pack) in a deep tiffin and pour over 500 ml just-boiled water until covered.
Lid on. Noodles soften in the heat without any stove.
In a mug, whisk the peanut butter, soy sauce, sugar, lemon juice, chilli flakes and 2 tablespoons of hot water into a pourable sauce.
Drain the noodles and rinse them once with tap water so they stop sticking together.
Toss the noodles in the peanut sauce until coated.
Top with thin cucumber sticks and sliced spring onion greens.

tip.text: Peanut butter seizes into a lump with cold liquid. Use hot water and whisk with a fork until glossy.

steps.text: Soak 50 g soya chunks in 500 ml boiling water with a pinch of salt, lid on.
Keep the lid on while the chunks puff up and turn spongy.
Cut the onion and capsicum into petal-sized squares, the way Chinese stalls do.
Drain the soya, rinse in cold water and squeeze each piece completely dry.
Stir the schezwan chutney with the soy sauce, then coat the soya chunks with it.
Fold in the onion and capsicum, which stay crunchy, and scatter spring onion on top.

tip.text: Schezwan chutney varies a lot in heat. Start with one spoon, taste a chunk, then add more.

steps.text: Put 1 egg in the empty kettle, cover with water and boil it.
Leave the egg in the hot water with the lid closed for a jammy centre.
Take the egg out into cold water. Empty the kettle and refill with 350 ml fresh water.
Add the noodle cake, half the tastemaker and the grated garlic, then boil twice, stirring in between.
Stir in the soy sauce and pour into a deep bowl with all the broth.
Peel and halve the egg, set it on top and finish with spring onion and sesame seeds.

tip.text: Using only half the tastemaker plus soy keeps the broth from being salt-bomb level. The egg needs the contrast.

steps.text: Peel a thumb-sized piece of ginger by scraping it with a spoon, then slice it thin.
Put the ginger slices and the tea leaves in a strainer over a big mug.
Pour 250 ml boiling water through and let it steep with a saucer on top.
Lift the strainer out and squeeze half a lemon into the mug.
Stir in the honey only after the tea has cooled for a minute.

tip.text: Honey in boiling water tastes flat and burnt. Let the tea drop off the boil first.

steps.text: Put 100 g frozen peas in a bowl and pour over enough boiling water to cover them.
Cover and let the peas thaw and warm through.
Chop the onion, tomato and coriander.
Drain the peas fully and lightly crush a third of them with the back of a spoon.
Mix in onion, tomato, chaat masala, chilli powder, salt and lemon juice.
Top with sev just before eating so it stays crunchy.

tip.text: Crushing some peas makes the masala cling. If you leave them all whole, the spices slide to the bottom of the bowl.

steps.text: Pour boiling water over 100 g frozen corn kernels in a mug.
Cover the mug with a saucer so the steam stays in.
Meanwhile chop the onion, tomato and coriander finely.
Drain the corn and shake the mug dry so the masala sticks.
Add chilli powder, chaat masala and salt, toss, then the onion, tomato and lemon juice.

tip.text: Wet corn makes a watery, bland chaat. Drain properly and pat with a clean tissue if needed.

steps.text: Put 120 g frozen corn into a steel tumbler and cover with boiling water from the kettle.
Lid it with a saucer and let the corn plump up.
Drain the water completely, keeping the corn in the tumbler.
Drop in 10 g butter straight away so the heat of the corn melts it.
Add salt and a generous amount of black pepper, cover, and shake the tumbler hard.
Squeeze a few drops of lemon on top, just like the mall corn cart.

tip.text: If the corn cools before the butter goes in, it won't melt. Work quickly after draining.

steps.text: Hard-boil 2 eggs in the kettle by covering them with water and switching it on.
Leave them in the hot water, lid shut.
Cool the eggs in tap water, peel and cut each one into quarters.
Mix the chopped onion, tomato, chilli and coriander in a bowl with salt and lemon juice.
Lay the egg quarters on a plate yolk-side up and spoon the onion-tomato mix over them.
Dust with chaat masala and scatter sev across everything.

tip.text: Peel under running water from the fat end, where the air pocket is. The shell comes off in big pieces.

steps.text: Put 60 g oats in a large mug and pour over 150 ml boiling water.
Cover and leave the oats to soften.
Slice the banana into coins while you wait.
Stir in 100 ml cold milk. It cools the oats to eating temperature and makes them creamy.
Swirl in the peanut butter so it melts in ribbons, then top with banana and honey.

tip.text: Never put milk in the kettle to save a step. It burns onto the element, smells for weeks and can ruin the kettle.

steps.text: Chop 3 dates and 8 almonds into small bits on a plate.
Put the oats and chopped dates in a mug and pour over 150 ml boiling water.
Cover. The dates soften and sweeten the oats so you need no sugar.
Stir in the cold milk until smooth.
Scatter the almonds on top for crunch.

tip.text: Add the dates now, not at the end. Soaking is what turns them jammy and spreads the sweetness.

steps.text: Soak 40 g soya chunks in boiling water, lid on, with a pinch of salt.
Keep the bowl covered while the chunks swell to double their size.
Drain, rinse in cold water and squeeze them bone dry.
Chop the soya on a board until it looks like mince (keema).
Mix the soya keema with mayo, ketchup, chilli powder, garam masala and chopped onion.
Lay lettuce on the wrap, spoon the keema down the middle, fold in the bottom and roll tightly.

tip.text: Chopping is the trick. Whole chunks fall out of a wrap. Keema-size bits hold in the mayo.

steps.text: Boil 2 eggs in the kettle, then leave them in the hot water with the lid closed.
Keep them in the closed kettle until the yolks are fully set.
Cool the eggs in cold water and peel them.
Mash the eggs with a fork in a bowl until there are no big white chunks left.
Stir in mayo, salt, pepper and finely sliced spring onion.
Spread thickly on one slice of bread, press the second slice on top and cut diagonally.

tip.text: Mash the eggs before adding mayo. If you mix both at once the yolk smears and the filling turns gluey.

steps.text: Put 2 eggs in the kettle with water and boil them.
Leave them in the closed kettle for hard-set yolks.
Lift the eggs out, then pour the still-hot kettle water over 100 g moong sprouts in a bowl.
Let the sprouts blanch so they lose the raw taste but keep their crunch.
Drain the sprouts and toss them with onion, tomato, chaat masala, salt and lemon.
Peel and slice the eggs into rounds and arrange them on top.

tip.text: Reusing the egg water is fine and saves power. Just don't drink it.

steps.text: Pour boiling water over 120 g moong sprouts in a tiffin.
Cover the tiffin so the sprouts soften slightly in the steam.
Drain and spread the sprouts on a plate for a minute so they stop cooking.
Mix with finely chopped onion, tomato, green chilli and coriander.
Season with chaat masala, salt and lemon juice.
Pile into a bowl and crown it with sev.

tip.text: More than 3 minutes and sprouts go soft and taste like boiled grass. Keep the crunch.

steps.text: Pour 320 ml water into the kettle and add the frozen peas and corn.
Boil once so the frozen vegetables thaw before the noodles go in.
Add the noodle cake broken in half and boil again.
Leave the lid shut so the noodles finish softening.
Open, stir in the tastemaker and boil one last time, watching for froth.
Pour into a bowl and drop the butter on top to melt.

tip.text: Frozen veg chills the water. If you add noodles to lukewarm water they turn soggy outside and hard inside.

steps.text: Put 70 g couscous in a bowl with a small pinch of salt.
Pour 100 ml boiling water over it.
Cover tightly with a plate and leave the grains to drink up the water.
Chop the pickle pieces small and keep 1 tablespoon of the pickle oil aside.
Fluff the couscous, then stir in the pickle oil until every grain glistens.
Add the chopped pickle, onion, peanuts and coriander and toss.

tip.text: Pickle is already very salty. Use only a pinch of salt in the water or the dish becomes inedible.

steps.text: Pour 120 ml boiling water over 45 g oats and cover.
Keep the oats covered until they are soft all the way through.
Uncover and let it sit until it is just warm, not hot.
Stir in the curd and salt until it looks like curd rice.
Grate the cucumber and ginger in, and add finely chopped green chilli.
Scatter pomegranate seeds and coriander on top.

tip.text: Curd stirred into hot oats splits and turns sour. Wait for the oats to cool down.

steps.text: Soak 40 g soya chunks in boiling water with a pinch of salt.
Keep the lid on until the chunks are puffy and pale.
Drain, rinse in cold water and squeeze out every drop.
Tear the chunks into small pieces with your fingers.
Whisk the curd with finely chopped mint, salt and chaat masala until smooth.
Fold in the soya, grated cucumber and onion. Chill it if you have a fridge.

tip.text: Warm soya in cold curd makes it watery. Rinse the chunks cold first.

steps.text: Steep 60 g couscous in 85 ml boiling water with a pinch of salt, covered.
Keep it covered until every grain is fluffy and the water is gone.
Fluff with a fork and spread it on a plate to cool.
Whisk the curd with salt and the cumin seeds crushed between your fingers.
Fold the cooled couscous into the curd with chopped cucumber and mint.
Finish with a handful of pomegranate seeds.

tip.text: Spreading the couscous on a plate cools it in 2 minutes. Left in the bowl, it stays hot for ages.

steps.text: Put the corn and sprouts together in a tiffin and pour boiling water over them.
Cover the tiffin and let the hot water blanch the corn and sprouts.
Drain and rinse with cold water so they stay bright.
Grate the carrot and dice the capsicum small.
Toss everything with olive oil, lemon juice, salt and pepper.

tip.text: The cold rinse is what keeps the corn yellow and sprouts green instead of dull and grey.

steps.text: Boil 2 eggs in the kettle and hold them in the hot water.
Keep the kettle lid shut until the yolks are firm.
Peel the eggs while still warm and chop them roughly.
Mix the warm egg with butter, turmeric, chilli powder and salt until the butter melts.
Fold in the finely chopped onion, tomato and chilli.
Pile the mash onto two slices of bread and eat open-faced.

tip.text: Do this while the eggs are warm. The butter needs that heat to melt and give the bhurji taste.

title: Kettle Couscous with Tuna and Lemon

steps.text: Pour 85 ml boiling water over 60 g couscous with a pinch of salt.
Cover the bowl with a plate and let the couscous steam.
Open half a can of tuna and drain the brine into the sink.
Fluff the couscous and stir in the olive oil.
Flake the tuna in with a fork and add diced cucumber.
Season with lemon juice, black pepper and chopped coriander.

tip.text: Keep the other half of the tuna in a closed container in the fridge and finish it within a day. Never store it in the open can.

steps.text: Put 50 g oats and a teaspoon of chia seeds into a jar or steel tumbler with a lid.
Pour in 150 ml cold milk and stir so no dry oats stick to the bottom.
Mash half the banana into the jar and stir again. Slice the other half and keep it for the morning.
Close the lid and put the jar in the fridge overnight, or at least 6 hours.
In the morning, stir, loosen with a splash of milk if thick, and top with banana slices and honey.

tip.text: Mashed banana goes brown on top overnight. That's fine to eat. The sliced half stays fresh only if you keep it whole until morning.

title: Overnight Oats with Dates and Peanut Butter

steps.text: Chop 3 pitted dates into tiny pieces so they melt into the oats overnight.
Stir oats, dates and peanut butter together in a jar until the peanut butter is broken up.
Pour in 160 ml cold milk and stir well, scraping the corners.
Lid on and into the fridge for the night.
Stir, then crush the almonds with the bottom of a glass and scatter them on top.

tip.text: Peanut butter needs the oats to break it up first. Add it to milk directly and you get a hard blob.

steps.text: Whisk 25 g chia seeds (about 2 tablespoons) into 180 ml cold milk with the honey.
Wait, then whisk again. This stops the seeds clumping at the bottom.
Cover and chill until thick and spoonable, ideally overnight.
Hull and chop the strawberries.
Spoon the pudding into a bowl and pile the strawberries on top.

tip.text: Skip the second whisk and you'll find a solid chia brick at the bottom and milk on top.

steps.text: Put 35 g sattu (about 3 tablespoons) in a tall glass with salt and chaat masala.
Add 3 tablespoons of water and stir into a smooth paste with no dry lumps.
Slowly pour in 250 ml cold water while stirring.
Squeeze in half a lemon and add very finely chopped onion, green chilli and torn mint.
Stir right before every sip, because sattu settles to the bottom.

tip.text: Dumping sattu into a full glass of water makes lumps that never dissolve. Paste first, then water.

steps.text: Grate or finely crush 60 g jaggery so there are no hard lumps.
Warm the ghee by standing its jar in a mug of hot water until it is liquid.
Mix sattu, jaggery and chopped almonds in a bowl with your fingers.
Pour in the melted ghee and rub it through until the mix holds a shape when squeezed.
Press portions into 8 tight balls, pushing a raisin into the top of each.
Store them in a closed box. Two laddoos make a decent snack.

tip.text: If the mix crumbles, add a teaspoon more ghee. Don't add water, it will make the laddoos spoil in a day.

steps.text: Chop the onion, tomato, green chilli and coriander small and keep them in separate heaps.
In a mixing bowl, stir the ketchup with lemon juice and chaat masala into a tangy sauce.
Add the onion, tomato, chilli and peanuts to the sauce and mix.
Tip in 40 g puffed rice and toss quickly with a spoon so every grain gets coated.
Top with sev and coriander and eat within 2 minutes.

tip.text: Puffed rice goes soggy in a few minutes. Mix it in only when you are ready to eat.

ingredients.note: mustard oil if you have it

steps.text: Put the puffed rice in a steel tiffin with a tight lid.
Add finely chopped onion, cucumber, green chilli and the peanuts.
Drizzle 1 teaspoon of oil over everything and sprinkle the chaat masala.
Close the lid and shake it hard for 20 seconds, the way the Kolkata muri-wallahs do in their tin.
Squeeze a little lemon, toss in coriander, and eat straight from a paper cone or the tiffin.

tip.text: Mustard oil gives the real sharp kick. Plain oil works but use a bit more green chilli to make up.

steps.text: Pour 50 g roasted chana into a bowl and pick out any bits of husk.
Dice the onion, tomato and cucumber to roughly the size of the chana.
Add the vegetables, chaat masala and chilli powder to the chana.
Squeeze half a lemon over and toss until the spices coat everything.
Finish with coriander. It keeps its crunch for about 15 minutes.

tip.text: Roasted chana is already salted in most packs. Taste one before adding any salt.

steps.text: Soak 40 g yellow moong dal in plenty of water. 2 hours is enough, all morning is fine too.
Drain the dal completely in a sieve and let it drip for a few minutes.
Finely dice the cucumber and grate the carrot.
Mix dal, cucumber, carrot, desiccated coconut and chopped green chilli in a bowl.
Add salt and lemon juice only just before eating, then the coriander.

tip.text: Salt pulls water out of cucumber. Add it early and you end up with a puddle at the bottom.

steps.text: Drain the chickpeas and rinse them under the tap until the water stops foaming.
Shake the sieve and spread the chickpeas on a cloth to dry for a minute.
Chop onion, tomato, green chilli and coriander finely.
Toss the chickpeas with chaat masala and salt first so the spice sticks.
Fold in the vegetables and pomegranate, then squeeze lemon over the top.

tip.text: The canning liquid tastes metallic and makes some people bloated. Rinse properly.

steps.text: Rinse 150 g canned rajma in a sieve and let it drain.
Dice the tomato, onion and capsicum small for a quick salsa.
Crush the cumin seeds between your palms and mix them with chilli powder, salt and lemon juice.
Toss the rajma and salsa vegetables in that dressing.
Top with a spoon of curd standing in for sour cream, and coriander.

tip.text: Raw cumin seeds taste harsh whole. Crushing them releases the flavour without needing to roast them.

steps.text: Drain half a can of tuna well, pressing the lid down on it over the sink.
Flake the tuna into a bowl and mix with mayo, very finely chopped onion and black pepper.
Add a few drops of lemon juice to cut the richness.
Slice the cucumber into thin rounds and lay them on one slice of bread.
Spread the tuna over the cucumber, close with the second slice and press down.

tip.text: Wet tuna makes soggy bread within minutes. Drain it until no more liquid comes out.

steps.text: Drain the tuna and flake it with a fork.
Stir the curd with lemon, salt and pepper to make a light dressing, then mix it into the tuna.
Shred the lettuce and slice the tomato into thin half-moons.
Lay the wrap flat, line it with lettuce, then tomato, then tuna down the centre.
Fold the bottom up first, then roll from one side tightly so nothing falls out.

tip.text: Folding the bottom first is what stops the filling dripping out when you bite in.

steps.text: Cut the avocado in half around the seed, twist apart and scoop the flesh into a bowl.
Mash it with a fork, leaving some chunks, and season with salt, pepper and half the lemon.
Spread the avocado thickly over two slices of sourdough, right to the edges.
Drape the smoked salmon in loose folds over the avocado.
Finish with chilli flakes and another squeeze of lemon over the fish.

tip.text: A ripe avocado yields slightly when pressed near the stem. Rock-hard ones need 2 to 3 days in a paper bag.

steps.text: Scoop the avocado into a bowl and mash with salt and lemon juice.
Slice the tomato into thin rounds and salt them lightly.
Spread the mash over the sourdough slices.
Layer the tomato rounds on top.
Drizzle with olive oil and shower with chilli flakes.

tip.text: Lemon in the mash isn't only flavour. It stops the avocado turning brown if you eat slowly.

steps.text: Spread 3 tablespoons of hummus over the whole wrap, leaving a 2 cm border.
Cut the cucumber into long thin sticks and grate the carrot.
Lay lettuce in a line across the middle and pile the cucumber, carrot and thin onion slices on it.
Squeeze a little lemon over the vegetables.
Roll it up tight and slice it on a diagonal.

tip.text: The border matters. Hummus right to the edge squeezes out the sides when you roll it.

steps.text: Spoon 170 g Greek yogurt into a wide bowl and smooth it with the back of the spoon.
Rinse the berries and pat them completely dry.
Halve the strawberries and scatter them with the blueberries over the yogurt.
Add the granola in one corner so it stays crunchy.
Drizzle honey in a thin line across the top.

tip.text: Wet berries water down the yogurt. Dry them on a tissue first.

steps.text: Cut the dragon fruit in half and scoop out the flesh with a spoon.
Dice half of it and mash the other half with the curd until bright pink.
Pour the pink curd into a bowl.
Arrange diced dragon fruit and banana slices in rows on top.
Finish with granola, chia seeds and honey.

tip.text: Dragon fruit tastes mild. Mashing it into the curd colours everything, and honey brings the sweetness.

steps.text: Spread the peanut butter across the whole wrap in a thin, even layer.
Peel the banana and lay it whole along one edge.
Drizzle honey and sprinkle sesame seeds over the peanut butter.
Roll the wrap tightly around the banana.
Cut it into 2 cm rounds like sushi pinwheels.

tip.text: A curved banana won't roll. Cut it in half lengthways and lay the pieces end to end.

steps.text: Cut 100 g fresh paneer into 1 cm cubes.
Toss the cubes with chaat masala, chilli powder and salt in a bowl.
Dice the onion, capsicum and tomato and add them.
Squeeze half a lemon over and toss gently so the paneer doesn't crumble.
Tear mint leaves over the top.

tip.text: Only use paneer bought in the last 2 days for raw chaat. Older paneer turns sour and rubbery.

steps.text: Rinse 50 g thick poha in a sieve and leave it to drain.
Whisk the curd with milk and salt until smooth and pourable.
Stir the poha into the curd and wait 5 minutes for it to soften.
Mix in grated cucumber, grated ginger and chopped green chilli.
Top with pomegranate seeds and coriander.

tip.text: Adding a little milk keeps the dish from turning sour if you eat it an hour later.

steps.text: Rinse 60 g thick poha once and let it sit in the sieve for 2 minutes.
Crush or grate the jaggery as fine as you can.
Put the poha in a bowl, pour the curd over and mix.
Sprinkle the jaggery over the top. Don't stir it in fully, the pockets of sweetness are the point.
Slice the banana on top and eat straight away.

tip.text: Big jaggery chunks won't melt in cold curd. Grate it or bash it inside a folded paper.

steps.text: Put the peanuts in a folded paper and crush them with the bottom of a steel glass to a coarse powder.
Peel and finely chop the cucumber, then squeeze it in your fist to remove excess water.
Mix the cucumber with crushed peanuts, coconut and chopped green chilli.
Season with sugar, salt and lemon juice.
Fold in coriander and eat it as a side or a light lunch.

tip.text: Unsqueezed cucumber floods the bowl and the peanuts turn soggy.

steps.text: Dice the papaya into cubes and add it to a bowl first, since it is the softest.
Core and dice the half apple with its skin on.
Slice the banana into thick coins.
Squeeze lemon over everything right away so nothing browns.
Sprinkle chaat masala and a pinch of salt, toss gently and finish with pomegranate.

tip.text: Apple and banana brown within minutes. Lemon goes on immediately, not at the end.

steps.text: Peel and seed the papaya and cut 200 g into cubes.
Stir the curd until smooth and spread it in a bowl.
Pile the papaya on top of the curd.
Chop the almonds roughly and scatter them over with the chia seeds.
Add honey only if the papaya isn't sweet.

tip.text: Papaya seeds are bitter. Scrape every one out with a spoon.

steps.text: Spread peanut butter edge to edge on both slices of bread.
Slice the banana into thin rounds, about 3 mm.
Lay the banana in overlapping rows on one slice.
Drizzle the honey over the banana.
Close the sandwich, press it flat with your palm and cut it in half.

tip.text: Spreading peanut butter on both slices stops the banana making the bread soggy.

steps.text: Chop the mint, coriander and green chilli together on a board for a full 3 minutes until it's almost a paste.
Scrape the herb paste into a bowl and stir in lemon juice and a pinch of salt for a rough green chutney.
Butter both slices of bread, then spread the chutney over the butter.
Layer thin cucumber and tomato rounds on one slice and sprinkle chaat masala over them.
Close, press down and cut into four triangles.

tip.text: Butter goes on before chutney. It stops the wet chutney from soaking straight into the bread.

steps.text: Pit the dates and chop them finely on a board, pressing with the knife until they form a sticky mass.
Chop the almonds into small pieces.
Knead the dates, almonds, oats and peanut butter together with your hands.
Roll the mix into 12 balls about the size of a large marble.
Roll each ball in desiccated coconut and keep them in a closed box.

tip.text: If the mix is too dry to hold, wet your hands slightly. If it's too sticky, add a spoon more oats.

steps.text: Mash the banana completely smooth with a fork in a bowl.
Add the sattu and grated jaggery and mix into a thick paste.
Spoon the paste into a bottle with a tight cap.
Pour in 250 ml cold milk, close the cap and shake for 30 seconds.
Drink right away, giving the bottle a shake between sips.

tip.text: Any banana lumps will block the bottle mouth. Mash until it's like baby food.

steps.text: Put 1.5 teaspoons instant coffee and the sugar into a bottle.
Add 2 tablespoons of warm tap water and swirl until the coffee dissolves into syrup.
Pour in 250 ml milk straight from the fridge.
Close tightly and shake hard for 40 seconds to get the cafe-style froth.
Pour over ice if you have it, or drink straight from the bottle.

tip.text: Instant coffee won't dissolve in cold milk. That little bit of warm water is not optional.

steps.text: Whisk the curd in a jug until completely smooth.
Add 400 ml cold water a little at a time, whisking between pours.
Grate in the ginger and add finely chopped mint and green chilli.
Season with chaat masala and salt.
Pour into two glasses. It's best within an hour.

tip.text: Pour all the water in at once and the curd forms lumps you'll never whisk out.

steps.text: Mash the banana with a fork until smooth.
Add the curd and honey to the banana and whisk hard for a minute.
Pour in the milk and whisk again until it is drinkable.
Taste and add a little more honey if your curd is sour.
Pour into a tall glass and drink right away.

tip.text: Curd from the fridge is mild. Curd left out all day gets sour and needs more honey.

steps.text: Rinse the rajma and lightly mash half of it with chilli powder and salt.
Chop the tomato, onion and capsicum and mix them with lemon juice for a salsa.
Spread the tortilla chips on a plate in a single layer.
Spoon the rajma over the chips, then the salsa.
Finish with blobs of curd and scattered grated cheese.

tip.text: Build it on a flat plate in one layer. Piled in a bowl, the bottom chips go soggy while the top ones stay bare.

title: Greek Yogurt Dip with Carrot Sticks

steps.text: Grate half a garlic clove into the yogurt.
Stir in oregano, salt and a squeeze of lemon.
Let the dip rest so the garlic mellows into it.
Cut the carrot and cucumber into finger-length sticks.
Dip and eat. Leftover dip keeps a day in a closed box in the fridge.

tip.text: Raw garlic gets stronger as it sits. Half a clove is plenty for one person.

steps.text: Crumble 60 g paneer between your fingers into a bowl.
Add mayo, finely diced capsicum, black pepper, oregano and salt.
Mix until the paneer is coated but still crumbly.
Spread the filling over one slice of bread right to the corners.
Close with the other slice, press, and cut in half.

tip.text: Mayo is salty already. Taste the filling before adding the salt.

steps.text: Rinse and drain the chickpeas, then pat them dry.
Smash the chickpeas roughly with a fork in a bowl.
Add half an avocado and mash again, leaving it chunky.
Season with lemon juice, salt, pepper and chilli flakes.
Pile it high on two slices of sourdough.

tip.text: Wrap the other avocado half with its seed in, cut side down on a plate, to slow browning until tomorrow.

steps.text: Dice the cucumber, tomato and onion into small even cubes, about 5 mm.
Finely chop the green chilli and coriander.
Tip all the chopped vegetables into one wide bowl.
Add salt, chaat masala and lemon juice right before eating.
Toss and eat it as a side with dal-rice, or with eggs for a light meal.

tip.text: Salt it early and the tomatoes weep. Season at the last second.

steps.text: Peel and grate the carrot and beetroot into a bowl.
Crush the peanuts coarsely inside a folded paper.
Stir the curd with salt and sugar until smooth.
Fold the grated vegetables and chopped green chilli into the curd.
Top with the crushed peanuts and a few drops of lemon.

tip.text: Beetroot stains hands and boards pink. Grate it last and rinse the board right away.

steps.text: Slice the banana into thin coins.
Spoon a third of the curd into a glass or jar.
Add a layer of granola, then banana.
Repeat the layers once more and finish with curd.
Drizzle honey and top with the last of the granola.

tip.text: Save some granola for the top. It's the only layer that stays crunchy.

steps.text: Finely chop the onion, tomato and coriander.
Mix them in a bowl with chilli powder, chaat masala and lemon juice.
Add the roasted peanuts and toss to coat them in the masala.
Fold in the plain cornflakes with a light hand so they don't crush to dust.
Top with sev and eat immediately.

tip.text: Use plain cornflakes, not the sugar-coated ones. Frosted bhel is a crime.

steps.text: Cut the cucumber into thick rounds, about 1 cm, and pat dry.
Mix the Greek yogurt with lemon juice, black pepper and very finely sliced spring onion.
Put a small dab of the yogurt on each cucumber round.
Tear the salmon into strips and fold one onto each round.
Grind a little extra pepper on top and eat them cold.

tip.text: Wet cucumber makes the toppings slide off. Pat each round dry.

steps.text: Rinse and drain the chickpeas.
Cut the cucumber and tomato into chunky cubes and slice the onion thin.
Whisk olive oil, lemon juice, oregano and salt in the bottom of a bowl.
Toss in the chickpeas and vegetables.
Crumble the paneer over the top with an extra pinch of salt, since feta is much saltier.

tip.text: Real feta is salty and sharp. Salted paneer plus extra lemon gets you close for a fraction of the price.

steps.text: Thaw the corn in a sieve under warm running tap water, then drain.
Dice the avocado and cucumber into 1 cm cubes.
Drain the tuna and flake it into large chunks.
Arrange tuna, avocado, cucumber and corn in sections in a bowl.
Dress with soy sauce and lemon juice, then sprinkle sesame and spring onion.

tip.text: Tap-warm water thaws frozen corn in a minute and makes it safe to eat raw. No cooking needed.

steps.text: Put the Greek yogurt in a bowl. It is already as thick as hung curd, so no draining overnight.
Add the sugar and whisk until it fully dissolves and the yogurt turns glossy.
Loosen with a spoon of milk if it's stiff.
Slice the almonds into thin slivers with a sharp knife.
Top with almonds and chill before eating.

tip.text: Undissolved sugar makes shrikhand gritty. Whisk until you can't feel grains on your tongue.

steps.text: Rinse 60 g thick poha in a sieve under the tap for 10 seconds, shake, and leave it to soften while you cook.
Heat 2 teaspoons oil in the pan on medium. Add mustard seeds and wait until they start popping.
Add curry leaves, slit green chilli and the peanuts and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the thinly sliced onion and cook until soft and see-through, not brown.
Stir in turmeric, then tip in the poha with salt and sugar and toss gently with a flat spoon.
Cover with a lid on low heat so the poha steams through.
Switch off, squeeze lemon over and scatter coriander.

tip.text: Never soak poha in a bowl of water. A short rinse in a sieve is enough. Soaked poha turns to mush the moment it hits the pan.

steps.text: Peel the potato and cut it into small 1 cm cubes so it cooks fast.
Rinse the poha in a sieve and let it drain.
Heat oil, crackle the mustard and cumin seeds, then add curry leaves and green chilli.
Add the potato with a pinch of salt and turmeric, cover with a lid and cook on low, stirring once.
When a potato cube breaks easily with the spoon, add the sliced onion and cook 2 minutes more.
Add the poha, sugar and remaining salt, toss, cover and leave on the lowest heat for 2 minutes.
Finish with lemon juice and coriander.

tip.text: Potatoes take longer than the poha. If you add them together, you get hard potato in mushy poha. Cook them first, covered.

steps.text: Dry roast 60 g rava in the pan on low heat, stirring, until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker.
Tip the rava onto a plate and wipe the pan.
Heat oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add peanuts, curry leaves, chopped green chilli and grated ginger.
Add the chopped onion and cook until soft, about 2 minutes.
Pour in 200 ml water with the salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and pour in the rava in a thin stream with one hand while stirring hard with the other.
Stir in the ghee, cover, and let it rest off the heat to fluff up.
Fluff with a fork and add a squeeze of lemon and coriander.

tip.text: Dump all the rava in at once and it forms lumps that stay raw inside. Pour slowly and keep stirring.

steps.text: Roast the rava dry on low heat until it smells toasty, then set it aside on a plate.
Heat oil, crackle mustard seeds, then add curry leaves, green chilli and onion.
Add the chopped tomatoes with salt and cook, pressing them, until they collapse into a pulp.
Stir in turmeric, chilli powder and sambar powder and cook 30 seconds.
Add 220 ml water and bring it to a boil.
Rain in the roasted rava while stirring constantly until it thickens.
Add ghee, cover and turn off the heat. Let it steam.

tip.text: The tomato must break down completely. Underdone tomato gives a sour, watery bath instead of a rich red one.

steps.text: If your vermicelli isn't roasted, toast it dry in the pan until golden, then tip it out.
Heat oil, add mustard seeds and wait for them to pop, then add curry leaves and chilli.
Add onion, finely diced carrot and peas and cook 3 minutes.
Pour in 180 ml water with salt and bring to a boil.
Add the vermicelli, stir once and cover on low heat until the water is absorbed.
Fluff with a fork to separate the strands and squeeze over the lemon.

tip.text: Stir only once. Constant stirring breaks the strands and you end up with semiya paste.

steps.text: The night before, rinse 75 g sabudana twice, then soak it in just enough water to cover the pearls.
In the morning, press a pearl between your fingers. It should squash fully with no hard centre.
Crush the peanuts coarsely and mix them into the sabudana with salt and sugar.
Heat ghee in a pan, add cumin seeds and green chilli, then the potato diced very small.
Cover and cook the potato on low until tender.
Add the sabudana and stir gently on medium heat until the pearls turn translucent.
Switch off, add lemon juice and coriander.

tip.text: Too much soaking water is the number one reason sabudana khichdi turns into a sticky lump. Water should just cover the pearls.

steps.text: Whisk 60 g besan with turmeric, chilli powder, salt and 90 ml water into a smooth batter, like thin pancake batter.
Stir in finely chopped onion, tomato, chilli and coriander.
Heat the pan on medium and smear half a teaspoon of oil over it with a folded tissue.
Pour half the batter in the centre and spread it outward in circles with the back of a ladle.
Drizzle a little oil around the edge and cook until the top looks dry.
Flip and cook the other side until golden spots appear.
Repeat with the remaining batter and eat with ketchup or curd.

tip.text: If the pan is too hot the batter sets before you can spread it. If too cold it sticks. Test with a drop of water: it should sizzle, not vanish.

steps.text: Rub the oats between your palms to break them into smaller flakes.
Mix oats, besan, curd, salt and cumin with 70 ml water.
Let the batter rest so the oats soften and thicken it.
Fold in finely chopped onion, capsicum and green chilli.
Spread a ladle of batter on a lightly oiled hot pan into a thick round.
Cook on medium-low until the bottom is golden and the edges lift.
Flip, press down with the spatula and cook another 2 minutes.

tip.text: Skipping the rest makes the chilla fall apart when you flip it. The oats need time to drink up the water.

steps.text: Crack 3 eggs into a bowl and beat with a fork for 30 seconds until no streaks of white remain.
Add the chopped onion, tomato, chilli, coriander, turmeric, chilli powder and salt and beat again.
Heat 2 teaspoons oil in the pan on medium and swirl it around.
Pour in the egg mix and tilt the pan so it spreads evenly.
Cook without touching until the edges set and the top is almost firm.
Fold it in half with the spatula, press for 20 seconds and slide onto a plate.

tip.text: Moving the eggs around turns an omelette into bhurji. Leave it alone until the edges set.

steps.text: Melt the butter in the pan on medium and add the chopped onion and green chilli.
Cook the onion until soft and just golden at the edges.
Add the tomato with turmeric, chilli powder and pav bhaji masala and cook until mushy.
Crack the eggs straight into the pan and stir everything continuously.
Keep scrambling on medium-low until the eggs are just set but still moist.
Stir in coriander and salt, then toast the pav on the hot pan for 30 seconds each side.

tip.text: Bhurji keeps cooking after you switch off. Take it off while it still looks slightly wet.

steps.text: Beat 2 eggs with chopped onion, green chilli, salt and pepper.
Melt half the butter in the pan and pour in the eggs, spreading them into a square-ish shape.
Dip both slices of bread quickly into the wet top of the omelette, then place them side by side on it.
Let the omelette set underneath.
Flip the whole thing so the bread is on the bottom and add the rest of the butter around it.
Fold the egg flaps over the bread, then fold the sandwich shut. Toast 30 seconds each side and serve with ketchup.

tip.text: Dipping the bread in the raw egg first is the street-stall trick that glues it all together.

steps.text: Whisk the eggs, milk and sugar in a wide plate.
Lay one slice of bread in the mix for 5 seconds per side, just long enough to soak, not fall apart.
Melt a little butter in the pan on medium.
Fry the soaked slice until golden brown underneath.
Flip with a wide spatula and brown the second side.
Repeat with the remaining slices, then top with banana slices and honey.

tip.text: Long soaking makes the centre soggy and eggy. A quick dip is enough for brown bread.

steps.text: Beat the eggs with turmeric, chilli powder, salt and 2 tablespoons water in a wide plate.
Stir in very finely chopped onion, chilli and coriander.
Heat a little oil in the pan on medium.
Dip a slice of bread on both sides, pressing some onion bits onto the surface.
Fry until crisp and golden underneath, then flip.
Cook all the slices the same way and cut diagonally. Eat with ketchup.

tip.text: The onion bits fall off unless you press them onto the soaked bread with a spoon.

steps.text: Melt the butter in the pan and add the finely chopped garlic for 20 seconds.
Add the roughly chopped spinach and a pinch of salt and stir until it wilts, about a minute.
Beat the eggs with salt and pepper and pour them over the spinach.
Cook on medium-low until the edges are set.
Tear the cheese slice over one half of the omelette.
Fold the other half over the cheese, cover the pan for 30 seconds so it melts, and slide out.

tip.text: Wet spinach leaks water into the eggs. Spin or shake it dry after washing.

steps.text: Slice the onion and cucumber thin, toss them with lemon, salt and chaat masala and set aside.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt.
Heat oil in the pan, pour in the eggs and spread them to the size of the wrap.
Immediately press the wrap on top of the wet egg so they stick together.
Cook until the egg sets, then flip so the wrap side toasts.
Slide it out egg side up, line it with the onion mix, chilli and ketchup and roll it tight in paper.

tip.text: Lay the wrap on while the egg is still raw on top. That's what fuses them into one roll.

steps.text: Take the batter out of the fridge 15 minutes early and stir in a pinch of salt if the pack isn't salted.
Heat the pan on medium-high, then sprinkle a few drops of water. When they sizzle away, wipe the pan with a damp cloth.
Pour a ladle of batter into the centre and spread it in quick circles outward to make a thin round.
Drizzle ghee on top and around the edges and cook until the bottom is golden and crisp.
Fold the dosa in half and lift it out.
Stir chopped green chilli and salt into the curd as a quick dip.

tip.text: A non-stick pan that is too hot or too cold both make dosa stick. The water-drop test tells you when it's right.

steps.text: Chop the onion, tomato, green chilli and coriander very fine and mix with a pinch of salt.
Heat the pan on medium and grease it with a teaspoon of oil.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it only slightly. Uttapam should be thick, about 1 cm.
Scatter half the vegetable mix on top and press it in with the ladle.
Drizzle oil around the edge, cover and cook until the top is set.
Flip and cook the vegetable side until it browns.
Make a second one with the rest.

tip.text: The lid helps the thick batter cook through. Without it the outside burns before the middle sets.

steps.text: Cube the potatoes small, cover with water in the pan and boil until soft.
Drain, wipe the pan and mash the potatoes roughly with a spoon.
Heat oil, pop mustard seeds, add curry leaves, green chilli and sliced onion and cook until soft.
Add turmeric, salt and the mashed potato with 3 tablespoons water. Mix into a soft masala and take it out.
Wipe the pan, heat it, then spread a thin dosa and drizzle ghee around it.
Cook until crisp and golden underneath.
Spoon the potato masala down the centre, fold both sides over and lift it out.

tip.text: Small cubes boil in 12 minutes. Whole potatoes in a pan without a pressure cooker take 30.

steps.text: Mash the banana smooth in a bowl.
Whisk in the egg and milk, then the atta and sugar until just combined. A few lumps are fine.
Heat the pan on medium-low and rub it with a little butter.
Pour a small ladle of batter for each pancake, about 10 cm wide.
Cook until bubbles appear on top and the edges look dry.
Flip and cook the second side.
Stack them and pour honey over.

tip.text: Atta browns faster than maida. Keep the heat medium-low or the outside burns while the middle stays raw.

steps.text: Crush the oats by rubbing them between your palms or rolling a bottle over them in a bag.
Mash the banana and beat in the eggs.
Stir in the crushed oats and let the batter sit for 3 minutes.
Grease the pan with butter on medium-low heat and drop spoonfuls of batter, spreading each slightly.
Cook until the underside is golden.
Flip carefully and cook another minute. Top with warmed peanut butter.

tip.text: These are delicate. Make them small, about the size of your palm, or they break when you flip.

steps.text: Dissolve the grated jaggery in 100 ml warm water.
Whisk the atta into the jaggery water until there are no lumps. It should coat a spoon.
Heat the pan on medium-low and grease it with ghee.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thin round. Sprinkle sesame on top.
Cook until the edges lift and the bottom is brown.
Flip and cook with a little more ghee.

tip.text: Jaggery burns fast. If the pan smokes, take it off the heat for 20 seconds before the next one.

steps.text: Butter one side of each bread slice thinly.
Toast the slices buttered side down in a hot pan until crisp.
Flip and toast the plain side for 30 seconds.
Spread peanut butter on the crisp side so it melts slightly.
Top with banana slices and a thread of honey.

tip.text: Spread it on the hot side. Warm peanut butter spreads easily and soaks the toast.

steps.text: Cut 4 slices of bread into small cubes, crusts included.
Heat oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add curry leaves and green chilli.
Add the onion and cook until soft, then the tomato until mushy.
Stir in turmeric, chilli powder and salt with 2 tablespoons of water.
Tip in the bread cubes and fold gently until every piece is coloured.
Keep on low heat until the bread is warmed through and slightly crisp at the edges.

tip.text: Too much water makes bread upma soggy. 2 tablespoons is enough to carry the masala.

steps.text: Heat oil and cook the sliced onion and capsicum until soft.
Add the chopped garlic and cumin and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped tomatoes, chilli powder and salt and simmer until thick and saucy.
Make two hollows in the sauce with the back of a spoon.
Crack an egg into each hollow and sprinkle with salt.
Cover and cook on low until the whites are set but the yolks are runny.
Scatter coriander and eat straight from the pan with bread for dipping.

tip.text: Watery sauce means the eggs float and spread. Simmer until a spoon dragged through leaves a trail.

steps.text: Grate a small garlic clove into the yogurt with salt and lemon and spread it in a shallow bowl.
Fill the pan with 5 cm water and heat until small bubbles rise but it doesn't boil.
Crack each egg into a cup, then slide it gently into the water.
Poach until the whites are set and the yolk wobbles.
Lift the eggs out with a slotted spoon, let them drain, and set them on the yogurt.
Empty the pan, melt the butter with chilli powder until foaming red, and spoon it over the eggs. Eat with sourdough.

tip.text: Rolling boiling water rips the egg white into strings. Keep it at a gentle shiver.

steps.text: Wipe the mushrooms with a damp tissue and slice them thin.
Melt half the butter in a hot pan and add the mushrooms in one layer.
Let them sit untouched until browned underneath, then stir.
Add the chopped garlic, salt, lots of pepper and oregano and cook 1 minute more. Scoop them out.
Butter the bread and toast it in the same pan until crisp.
Lay half a cheese slice on each toast and pile the hot mushrooms on top so the cheese melts.

tip.text: Stirring mushrooms early or crowding the pan makes them steam grey and rubbery. Space and patience.

steps.text: Mix the rava, curd, salt and 80 ml water into a thick batter.
Rest the batter so the rava swells.
Stir in finely chopped onion, capsicum, grated carrot and chilli. Loosen with a splash of water if it's too thick to spread.
Heat a greased pan on medium and spread a ladle of batter into a round about 5 mm thick.
Cook covered until the top looks set.
Flip, drizzle oil around and cook until speckled brown.

tip.text: Unrested rava batter feels gritty and the cheela cracks. Ten minutes makes the difference.

steps.text: Crumble the paneer with your fingers into small pieces.
Melt butter and cook the onion and green chilli until soft.
Add tomato, capsicum, turmeric and chilli powder and cook until the tomato breaks down.
Add the paneer, salt and garam masala and stir to coat everything.
Cook just until the paneer is hot through.
Stir in coriander and eat with bread or wraps.

tip.text: Paneer turns rubbery if cooked long. Two minutes after it goes in is all it needs.

steps.text: Pat the tofu dry with a cloth and crumble it with a fork.
Heat the oil and soften the chopped onion and garlic.
Add the tofu with turmeric and salt and stir until it's yellow all over and hot.
Let it fry without stirring so some bits catch and turn golden.
Fold in the chopped spinach and stir until it just wilts.
Finish with soy sauce and black pepper.

tip.text: Wet tofu steams instead of browning. Press it in a cloth with something heavy for 5 minutes.

steps.text: Heat oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the onion and cook 2 minutes.
Add tomato, peas, turmeric, chilli powder and salt and cook until the tomato softens.
Push everything to the side, crack the eggs into the empty space and scramble them until just set.
Stir the eggs into the masala, then add the oats and 180 ml water.
Simmer, stirring, until the oats are creamy and thick.
Top with coriander. Add a splash of water if it thickens too much while you eat.

tip.text: Scrambling the eggs separately keeps them in proper bits instead of disappearing into the porridge.

steps.text: Rinse the poha in a sieve and let it drain.
Heat ghee, add cumin seeds, grated ginger and green chilli.
Add the frozen peas with a pinch of salt, cover and cook until tender.
Mash a few of the peas lightly with the back of the spoon.
Add the poha, sugar and remaining salt and toss on low heat until hot.
Finish with lemon juice and coriander.

tip.text: Mashing some peas gives the dish its creamy Banarasi texture instead of separate peas and poha.

steps.text: Melt half the butter in the pan, add garlic and spinach, and wilt for a minute. Season and take it out.
Butter and toast the bread in the same pan until crisp, then set it aside.
Fill the pan with water and bring it to a bare simmer.
Crack each egg into a cup, stir the water to make a gentle swirl, and slide the egg into the centre.
Poach until the white is opaque but the yolk is soft.
Pile spinach on the toast, top with the drained eggs and grind pepper over.

tip.text: Lift the egg out and rest the spoon on a tissue for 5 seconds. Poaching water makes toast soggy.

steps.text: Toast the bread on one side only in a little butter, then flip it toasted side up onto the board.
Lay a cheese slice on each toast and scatter chopped green chilli and onion over it.
Return the toasts to the pan, cheese side up, cover with a lid and cook until the cheese melts.
Take the toasts out and fry two eggs sunny side up in the rest of the butter.
Cook the eggs until the whites are fully set.
Slide an egg onto each cheese toast and sprinkle salt over the yolk.

tip.text: The lid melts the cheese without burning the bread. No lid means burnt bottom and cold cheese.

steps.text: Peel the sweet potato and cut it into 1 cm dice.
Fry the dice in oil with a pinch of salt, covered, stirring now and then until tender.
Uncover, add the onion and capsicum and fry until the potato edges crisp.
Season with chilli powder, salt and pepper.
Make two wells in the hash and crack an egg into each.
Cover and cook until the egg whites are set.

tip.text: The lid steams the sweet potato soft first. Then you crisp it with the lid off. Do it the other way round and it burns.

steps.text: Warm the milk with 100 ml water in a cup and keep it ready next to the stove.
Melt the ghee in the pan and fry the cashews and raisins until the raisins puff. Lift them out.
Add the rava to the ghee and roast on low, stirring, until golden and fragrant.
Carefully pour in the warm milk-water. It will splutter, so stand back.
Stir until the rava absorbs the liquid, then add the sugar.
Keep stirring until the sheera leaves the sides of the pan.
Fold in the cashews and raisins.

tip.text: Cold liquid makes the rava seize into lumps. Warm it first.

steps.text: Slice the mushrooms and fry them in half the butter on high until golden.
Season the mushrooms with salt and pepper and tip them onto a plate.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and add the remaining butter to the pan on medium.
Pour in the eggs and drag the edges into the middle a few times as they set.
When the top is still slightly wet, scatter the mushrooms, cheese and spring onion over one half.
Fold and let it sit 30 seconds so the cheese melts.

tip.text: Cooking mushrooms separately stops them leaking water into the eggs.

steps.text: Beat the egg with the finely chopped onion, tomato, green chilli, chilli powder, salt and coriander.
Spread the egg mixture thickly on one side of each bread slice.
Melt butter in the pan and place the slices egg side down.
Cook on medium until the egg layer is set and golden.
Flip and toast the plain side until crisp.
Cut each slice into strips for dipping in ketchup.

tip.text: Place the slices egg side down in one move. Hesitate and the topping slides off onto the pan.

steps.text: Rinse 100 g masoor dal in the pan three times until the water runs almost clear.
Add 450 ml water and turmeric, bring to a boil, then simmer half covered, stirring now and then, until the dal is soft and falling apart.
Whisk the dal with a spoon to make it creamy and add the salt. Pour it into a bowl or tiffin.
Wipe the pan and heat the ghee. Add cumin seeds and wait until they sizzle and darken slightly.
Add chopped garlic, ginger, onion and green chilli and fry until the onion is golden.
Add the chopped tomato and chilli powder and cook until the tomato turns soft and oily.
Pour the dal back into the pan, stir, simmer 2 minutes and finish with coriander.

tip.text: Masoor dal froths up and boils over the moment you look away. Keep the lid half open and the heat at medium-low.

steps.text: Rinse the moong dal and soak it in water while you chop everything else.
Drain, add 500 ml fresh water and turmeric, and simmer half covered until completely soft.
Whisk the dal smooth and add chopped tomato, grated ginger, jaggery and salt.
Simmer until the tomato softens and the jaggery melts in.
In a small steel cup on the side of the hob, or by pushing the dal aside, heat ghee and pop mustard seeds with hing, curry leaves and chilli.
Pour the tempering into the dal, switch off and squeeze in the lemon.

tip.text: Lemon added while the dal is boiling turns bitter. Squeeze it in after switching off.

steps.text: Wash the rice and moong dal together twice and soak them in water.
Heat the ghee in the pan, add cumin, hing and grated ginger and let them sizzle.
Drain the rice and dal and stir them into the ghee for a minute.
Add 700 ml water, turmeric, salt and the peas and bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer, stirring every 5 minutes so the bottom doesn't catch.
Mash a little with the spoon. It should be soft and porridge-like, so add hot water if it's too thick.
Eat with curd and a spoon of ghee on top.

tip.text: Khichdi thickens a lot as it cools. Stop when it looks slightly looser than you want.

steps.text: Wash the rice and dal together and soak them.
Heat ghee, pop mustard seeds, add curry leaves and peanuts, then the onion.
Add the diced carrot, beans and peas and stir for 2 minutes.
Add the tomato and sambar powder and cook until the tomato collapses.
Add the drained rice and dal, 800 ml water, salt and jaggery. Bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer on low, stirring every few minutes and scraping the bottom.
Squeeze in the lemon and stir. The texture should be soft and pourable.

tip.text: Masoor and rice love to stick. Scrape the bottom each time you stir or you'll get a burnt layer.

steps.text: Wash 80 g rice in three changes of water and leave it to soak.
Heat oil, pop mustard seeds, add curry leaves, chilli and onion and cook until golden.
Add the chopped tomato, chilli powder, turmeric and salt and cook down into a thick paste.
Add the drained rice and garam masala and stir gently for a minute to coat.
Pour in 170 ml water and bring to a boil.
Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat until the water is absorbed.
Switch off and leave the lid on to steam.

tip.text: Tomato adds its own liquid, so use a little less water than plain rice. 1 part rice to just over 2 parts water by volume, minus a bit.

steps.text: Wash the rice, then cook it with 180 ml water and a pinch of salt in the covered pan on low heat.
Spread the cooked rice on a plate to cool for 10 minutes so the grains firm up.
Wipe the pan, heat the oil and fry the peanuts until they darken a shade.
Add mustard seeds, hing, curry leaves and slit chilli, then the turmeric.
Switch off the heat and squeeze in the lemon juice.
Add the rice and salt and fold gently until every grain is yellow.

tip.text: Hot, fresh rice breaks into mush when you mix it. Cooled rice stays in separate grains.

steps.text: Cook the washed rice with 220 ml water, covered, until very soft.
Mash the rice while it's hot with the back of the spoon.
Let it cool until just warm, then stir in the milk, curd and salt.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds and add curry leaves, chilli and grated ginger.
Pour the tempering over the curd rice and mix.
Top with grated cucumber and pomegranate.

tip.text: Adding curd to hot rice makes it split and go sour. The milk keeps it mild for hours.

steps.text: Cook the rice with 160 ml water until just done, then spread it on a plate to cool and dry.
Heat oil on high, add the beaten eggs and scramble until just set. Push them aside.
Add the chopped garlic, carrot and capsicum and stir-fry on high for 2 minutes.
Add the cold rice and break up any clumps with the spoon.
Pour soy sauce around the edge of the pan, not on the rice, and toss.
Add pepper, salt and spring onion greens and toss for a final minute.

tip.text: Fresh hot rice turns sticky in a wok. Day-old or cooled rice gives you proper restaurant fried rice.

steps.text: Cook the rice in 160 ml water with a few drops of oil, then cool it fully on a plate.
Shred the cabbage and cut the carrot and beans into thin matchsticks.
Heat oil until it just smokes and toss the garlic for 10 seconds.
Add all the vegetables and stir-fry on maximum heat. They should stay crunchy.
Add the rice, soy sauce, sugar, salt and pepper and toss until the rice is hot and coloured.
Fold in spring onion and switch off.

tip.text: Most induction plates need the highest setting for stir-fry. Medium heat stews the vegetables.

steps.text: Cook the rice in 160 ml water, then spread it out to cool.
Cut the paneer into small cubes and fry them in half the oil until golden on two sides. Take them out.
Add the rest of the oil and stir-fry the diced onion and capsicum on high for a minute.
Stir in the schezwan chutney and soy sauce and let it sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the rice and paneer and toss until everything is red and coated.
Finish with sliced spring onion greens and eat straight away.

tip.text: Schezwan chutney burns quickly on high heat. Have the rice ready to go in right after.

steps.text: Cook the washed rice in 170 ml water, covered on low, then move it into a tiffin with the lid on.
Rinse the canned rajma and keep 2 tablespoons aside to mash.
Heat ghee, add cumin, then the chopped onion. Cook until deep golden.
Add garlic, ginger, tomato and the powdered spices and cook until the oil separates at the edges.
Add the rajma, the mashed spoonfuls and 200 ml water.
Simmer until the gravy turns thick and creamy.
Finish with garam masala and coriander and spoon it over the rice.

tip.text: Deep golden onion is where rajma flavour comes from. Pale onion gives you a thin, sweet gravy.

steps.text: Rinse the chickpeas and drain well.
Heat oil, add cumin, then the finely chopped onion, and cook until golden brown.
Add grated garlic and ginger and fry 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomato and powdered spices and cook until it's a thick masala.
Add the chickpeas and 150 ml water and crush a few against the pan to thicken the gravy.
Simmer until the gravy coats the back of a spoon.
Squeeze lemon on top and toast the pav in the pan for a minute.

tip.text: Mashing a few chickpeas thickens the gravy naturally without cream.

steps.text: Peel and cube the potatoes, then boil them with the peas in the pan with water until very soft.
Drain, keeping half a cup of the water, and mash everything with a steel glass bottom.
Wipe the pan, melt half the butter, and fry half the onion with the garlic until soft.
Add capsicum and tomato and cook, mashing, until the tomato disappears.
Add pav bhaji masala, chilli powder and salt, then the mashed vegetables and the cooking water.
Simmer and keep mashing until smooth and thick.
Slit the pav, toast it in the remaining butter, and serve with raw onion, lemon and coriander.

tip.text: Mashing is the bhaji. Keep going until you can't see any potato cubes.

steps.text: Heat oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add curry leaves and onion and cook until soft.
Add the desiccated coconut and roast with the onion until lightly brown.
Add tomato, turmeric, chilli powder and garam masala and cook until mushy.
Add the sprouts, salt, jaggery and 200 ml water.
Cover and simmer until the sprouts are tender but not mushy.
Finish with lemon and eat with toasted pav, or top with sev for a quick misal.

tip.text: Overcooked sprouts lose their bite. Taste one at 8 minutes.

steps.text: Peel the potatoes and cut them into 2 cm cubes.
Heat oil, add cumin, then the onion, and cook until golden.
Add grated ginger, tomato and the powdered spices except garam masala, and cook until oily.
Add the potatoes and stir to coat them in the masala for 2 minutes.
Add 400 ml water and the peas, cover and simmer until a potato cube breaks easily.
Crush a few potato pieces to thicken the gravy, then add garam masala and coriander.

tip.text: Without a pressure cooker the cubes need to be small. Big chunks will still be raw after 30 minutes.

steps.text: Boil the potato cubes in salted water in the pan until just tender.
Drain and let them steam dry for 2 minutes.
Heat the oil and add a full teaspoon of cumin until it crackles and darkens.
Add green chilli, turmeric and chilli powder, then the potatoes.
Fry on medium, turning occasionally, until edges are crisp.
Toss with chaat masala and coriander and roll into the warmed wraps with a spoon of curd.

tip.text: Wet potatoes splatter and never crisp. Let the steam escape before frying.

steps.text: Wash the spinach well and wilt it in the dry pan with its own water clinging to it.
Tip it out and chop it on a board as finely as you can, almost to a paste.
Heat ghee, add cumin, then chopped onion, garlic, ginger and chilli. Cook until soft.
Add the tomato and cook until it melts into the onion.
Add the chopped spinach, salt and 80 ml water and simmer 5 minutes.
Stir in the paneer cubes, garam masala and cream and simmer 2 more minutes.

tip.text: No blender? A sharp knife and 3 minutes of chopping gets you a rustic palak that tastes just as good.

steps.text: Soak the cashews in hot water and then crush them to a paste with a spoon.
Melt the butter and cook the chopped onion, garlic and ginger until soft.
Add the finely chopped tomatoes and cook, mashing, until they turn into a smooth paste.
Add chilli powder, the cashew paste, salt, sugar and 100 ml water.
Simmer for 3 minutes, then stir in the cream.
Add the paneer cubes and garam masala and crush the kasuri methi between your palms over the pan.

tip.text: The tomatoes must cook down fully or the gravy tastes raw and sour. Keep mashing until no pieces are left.

steps.text: Cut the capsicum and half the onion into chunky squares. Chop the other half fine.
Fry the onion and capsicum squares in a little oil on high for 2 minutes until charred at the edges. Take them out.
In the same pan, cook the chopped onion, garlic and ginger until golden.
Add the tomato and spice powders and cook until it turns into a thick masala.
Add the paneer, the charred vegetables and a splash of water.
Toss for 2 minutes and finish with crushed kasuri methi.

tip.text: Charring the capsicum separately keeps it crunchy and smoky, the way the dhaba version tastes.

steps.text: Whisk the curd with chilli powder, garam masala, grated ginger and garlic, besan, salt and half the lemon.
Cut the paneer, capsicum and onion into large cubes and coat them in the marinade.
Leave the paneer to marinate so the masala sinks in.
Heat the oil on high and lay the pieces in one layer.
Let them char without moving, then turn each piece.
Sprinkle chaat masala and squeeze the rest of the lemon on top.

tip.text: A crowded pan steams the tikka pale. Cook in two batches if you need to.

steps.text: Heat oil, add cumin, and cook the chopped onion until golden.
Add grated ginger, then tomato and all the powders except garam masala.
Cook until the masala thickens and oil appears at the edges.
Add the peas and 200 ml water and simmer until the peas are soft.
Add the paneer cubes and garam masala and simmer 2 minutes.
Scatter chopped coriander over the curry before eating.

tip.text: Oil separating from the masala is your signal it's cooked. Add water before that and the curry tastes raw.

steps.text: Hard-boil the eggs in the pan with water to cover.
Cool, peel and score each egg with 3 shallow cuts so the gravy gets in.
Dry the pan, heat oil and fry the eggs with a pinch of turmeric and chilli until blistered. Take them out.
Add cumin and the onion to the same oil and cook until deep brown.
Add garlic, ginger, tomato and the powdered spices and cook until thick.
Add 200 ml water and the eggs and simmer until the gravy thickens.
Finish with garam masala and coriander.

tip.text: Frying the boiled eggs gives them a skin that holds the masala. Plain boiled eggs in gravy taste bland.

steps.text: Hard-boil the eggs in the pan, then peel them.
Slice the onions thin. This dish needs a lot of onion.
Heat the oil and cook the onion with a pinch of salt on medium until soft and caramel brown.
Add crushed ginger, garlic, green chilli and curry leaves and fry 1 minute.
Add the spice powders and fry for 30 seconds until they smell toasty.
Add the tomato and cook until it melts into a dark, thick roast.
Add the eggs and a splash of water and turn them until fully coated.

tip.text: The onion needs the full 12 minutes. Rushing it on high heat burns the edges while the middle stays raw.

steps.text: Boil the eggs and quartered potatoes together in the pan until the potatoes are just tender.
Peel the eggs. Rub turmeric and salt over the eggs and potato pieces.
Fry them in hot oil until golden spots appear, then take them out.
In the same oil, add cumin, then grated onion and ginger, and cook until brown.
Add tomato, chilli powder and sugar and cook until oily.
Add the eggs, potatoes and 250 ml water and simmer until the gravy is thin but flavourful.
Sprinkle garam masala over the curry and rest it 2 minutes.

tip.text: Keep a lid in hand when frying the eggs. Boiled eggs can pop and spit hot oil.

steps.text: Cut the chicken into bite-size pieces and mix with curd, turmeric and half the salt.
Heat oil, add cumin and cook the onion until deep golden.
Add the grated garlic and ginger and fry until the raw smell goes.
Add the tomato and powdered spices and cook until the oil separates.
Add the chicken and fry it in the masala on medium-high until it turns white all over.
Add 200 ml water, cover and simmer until the chicken is cooked through.
Finish with garam masala and coriander. Cut a piece open: no pink inside.

tip.text: Boneless breast dries out fast. Cut one piece open at 12 minutes and stop as soon as there's no pink.

steps.text: Cut the chicken into 3 cm chunks.
Mix the curd with chilli powder, garam masala, grated ginger and garlic, lemon juice and salt.
Coat the chicken and leave it to marinate, longer in the fridge if you can.
Heat the oil until it's very hot and add the chicken in one layer, shaking off extra marinade.
Sear without moving, then turn each piece and cook the other sides.
Cut a thick piece open to check it's white all the way through, then dust with chaat masala and eat with onion rings.

tip.text: Too much marinade in the pan turns it into a curry. Shake each piece before it goes in.

steps.text: Cut the chicken into small pieces and toss with turmeric and salt.
Heat oil and fry the curry leaves until crisp, then add the sliced onion.
Cook the onion until golden, then add crushed garlic, ginger and green chilli.
Add the chicken and stir-fry on high until it browns at the edges.
Add coriander powder and a splash of water, cover and cook through.
Uncover, add all the pepper and toss on high until the pan is dry and the chicken is coated.

tip.text: Add the pepper at the end. Long-cooked pepper turns bitter instead of hot and fragrant.

steps.text: Toss the chicken pieces with curd, half the chilli powder and salt and leave them while you start the gravy.
Fry the chicken in half the butter on high until browned. Take it out.
In the same pan, cook the garlic and ginger in the rest of the butter for 30 seconds.
Add the finely chopped tomato and the crushed cashews and cook into a smooth paste.
Add the remaining chilli powder, sugar and 100 ml water and simmer 3 minutes.
Return the chicken, stir in the cream and simmer until cooked through.
Finish with garam masala and crushed kasuri methi.

tip.text: Once cream goes in, keep it at a gentle simmer. A hard boil splits it.

steps.text: Boil the soya chunks in water in the pan with a pinch of salt.
Drain, rinse in cold water and squeeze completely dry.
Heat oil, add curry leaves and onion and cook until golden.
Add ginger, garlic, tomato and all the powders and cook until thick.
Add the coconut, the soya chunks and 200 ml water.
Simmer so the chunks soak up the gravy.

tip.text: Squeeze the chunks dry so they absorb the curry instead of staying full of plain water.

steps.text: Boil the soya chunks for a few minutes, then drain, rinse cold and squeeze dry.
Chop the soya into fine mince on a board.
Heat oil and cook onion, garlic and ginger until golden.
Add tomato, chilli powder and pav bhaji masala and cook until mushy.
Add the soya mince, peas, salt and 100 ml water and cook until the peas are soft and the keema is dry.
Toast the pav in butter and eat with the keema and a squeeze of lemon.

tip.text: Mince it fine. Chunky soya won't feel like keema and won't take the masala.

steps.text: Boil the soya chunks, drain, rinse cold and squeeze bone dry.
Toss them with besan and a pinch of salt so they're lightly coated.
Shallow-fry the chunks in the oil until crisp on the outside.
Push them aside and stir-fry garlic, chilli, onion and capsicum squares on high for a minute.
Add soy sauce, ketchup and schezwan with 2 tablespoons of water.
Toss the soya in the sauce until glossy and finish with spring onion.

tip.text: The besan coat is what makes them crisp. Without it, soya stays soft and chewy.

steps.text: Soak the washed rice. At the same time soak the soya chunks in hot water.
Squeeze the soya dry and cut each chunk in half.
Heat ghee, add cumin and the sliced onion and cook until golden.
Add ginger, chilli, carrot, peas, soya and garam masala and stir 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice, 170 ml water and salt and bring to a boil.
Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat.
Rest with the lid on, then fluff and serve with curd.

tip.text: Don't lift the lid while the rice cooks. Every peek lets steam out and leaves the top layer hard.

steps.text: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then soak it.
Heat ghee and fry the cashews until golden, then add cumin and the sliced onion.
Add the diced beans, carrot and peas with garam masala and stir for 2 minutes.
Drain the rice and add it, stirring gently so the grains don't break.
Add 170 ml water, salt and torn mint and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest setting.
Switch off and rest without opening.

tip.text: Soaked rice cooks evenly and the grains stay long. Unsoaked rice in a pan cooks unevenly.

steps.text: Cut the cauliflower into small florets and the potato into small cubes.
Heat oil, add cumin, then the potato. Fry 3 minutes.
Add the cauliflower, turmeric and salt and toss well.
Cover and cook on low, stirring every few minutes, until both are tender.
Uncover, add onion, ginger, tomato and the spice powders and cook on medium until dry.
Finish with garam masala and coriander.

tip.text: Don't add water. The vegetables steam in their own moisture under the lid and stay whole.

steps.text: Blanch the florets in boiling salted water, then drain and pat dry.
Make a thick batter with besan, atta, chilli powder, salt and a little water and coat the florets.
Shallow-fry them in the oil, turning, until crisp on all sides.
Push them aside and fry chopped garlic, ginger and chilli, then onion and capsicum for a minute.
Add soy sauce, ketchup and 3 tablespoons of water and let it bubble.
Toss the cauliflower through and finish with spring onion.

tip.text: Toss the florets in the sauce only at the end. They go soft within minutes in the sauce.

steps.text: Cook the washed rice with 150 ml water, covered, and set it aside in a tiffin.
Shred the cabbage finely with a knife.
Heat oil, pop the mustard seeds, add curry leaves and slit chilli.
Add the cabbage, peas, turmeric and salt, cover and cook on low until tender but still bright.
Toss in the coconut and cook uncovered for a minute.
Eat with the rice and a spoon of pickle.

tip.text: Overcooked cabbage turns sulphury. Stop while it still has a little bite.

steps.text: Boil the potatoes in small cubes in the pan until soft.
Drain and roughly break them with the spoon. Leave some chunks.
Heat oil, pop mustard seeds, add hing, curry leaves, chilli and sliced onion.
When the onion softens, add turmeric and the potatoes with salt.
Stir gently for 2 minutes until everything is yellow and hot.
Finish with lemon and coriander and eat with pav.

tip.text: Breaking the potatoes, not mashing them, keeps the dry bhaji texture you get with puri.

steps.text: Pick the methi leaves off the stems, wash them and chop roughly.
Sprinkle a pinch of salt over the methi and leave it 5 minutes, then squeeze out the water to cut the bitterness.
Heat oil, add cumin and chopped garlic, then the potato cubes and turmeric.
Cover and cook on low, stirring now and then, until the potatoes are soft.
Add the methi, chilli powder and salt and stir-fry until the leaves wilt and dry out.
Warm the wraps in the dry pan and roll the methi aloo inside.

tip.text: Methi is bitter. The salt-and-squeeze step tames it, and the potatoes balance the rest.

steps.text: Melt the butter and cook the chopped onion, garlic and finely diced carrot for 4 minutes.
Add the cumin and chilli powder and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the rinsed masoor dal and 600 ml water.
Simmer half covered until the lentils and carrot are completely soft.
Whisk hard with a spoon or masher until the soup is almost smooth. Season with salt.
Squeeze a lot of lemon into each bowl and eat with bread.

tip.text: The lemon is not optional. Without it the soup tastes flat.

steps.text: Cook the washed rice with 300 ml water in the covered pan and transfer it to a tiffin.
Crush the garlic, pepper and cumin together inside a folded paper with a steel glass.
Squash the tomatoes by hand into the pan with turmeric, salt and 500 ml water.
Add the crushed spice mix and simmer until the tomatoes fall apart.
Heat the ghee in a ladle or push aside, crackle mustard seeds, hing and curry leaves and add to the rasam.
Switch off, add lemon and coriander, and pour over hot rice.

tip.text: Rasam should never boil hard after the tempering. It loses its fragrance.

steps.text: Simmer the rinsed masoor dal with 500 ml water and turmeric until soft.
Mash the dal and add the onion, tomato, carrot and beans.
Add sambar powder, salt, jaggery and 200 ml more water and simmer until the vegetables are tender.
Heat the oil in a ladle held over the plate, or in the pan pushed to one side, and pop mustard seeds with hing and curry leaves.
Pour the tempering into the sambar.
Squeeze in lemon in place of tamarind and eat with rice or dosa.

tip.text: Masoor is the shortcut. It cooks in 15 minutes in a pan, where toor dal needs a pressure cooker.

steps.text: Cook the rice with 300 ml water and keep it covered in a tiffin.
Whisk the curd and besan with 500 ml water, turmeric and salt until there are no lumps.
Heat the ghee in the pan and crackle cumin and mustard seeds, then add onion, ginger and chilli.
Pour in the besan mixture and stir constantly until it comes to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer, stirring every few minutes, until thick and smooth.
Dust chilli powder on top and pour over rice.

tip.text: Stop stirring before it boils and the curd splits into grainy bits. Stir until the first bubbles.
